## 🗺️ A map in a card

**Place** takes any of three things:

- a **coordinate** — `48.8584, 2.2945` (degrees and N/S/E/W are fine: `48.8584° N, 2.2945° E`)
- a **Wikidata item** — `Q64` (Berlin)
- a **page title** — `Brandenburg Gate`. A title is read from that wiki first, following redirects, and only then from its Wikidata item.

The map is drawn by **Wikimedia's own map service** at the size this card actually is, so it needs no tiles and no map library — and because it is one image it also **prints** and **exports to PNG** properly, where a tiled map would not. The service draws no marker of its own, so the **pin is ours**, at the centre — which is the coordinate you asked for. **Map label language** blank means your own browser's.

Set **Frame → Edge to edge** for a chrome-free map, **⛶** in its title bar to fill the screen, and click the map to open the same place on **OpenStreetMap**.

**Points** take the same vocabulary, one per line (up to 100): a coordinate, a Wikidata item, or a page title. With **Frame the points** on, the centre and the zoom are computed to fit them — the card below shows four Berlin landmarks, drawn at their own pixels by an SVG overlay that mirrors the image's own `object-fit`. A point the crop takes away is counted on the card rather than quietly dropped.

**The same list can draw a shape:** set **The points draw** to *A path* (a line through them, in order) or *An area* (a polygon — the ring is closed for you). Geometry also arrives **from another widget** (a map card publishes what it draws as GeoJSON; pick it in *Geometry from another widget*) or as **pasted GeoJSON** — RFC 7946, the format every map and drawing library speaks. Rings are closed for you, swapped axes are detected, style hints are ignored, and a shape that cannot be read says why instead of drawing nothing.
